entry: Electronic device that outputs a video signal to play video games, typically with a game controller. Home consoles stay in a fixed location and connect to a television or other display, while handheld consoles include their own screens; hybrid consoles combine both. The first consoles appeared in the early 1970s, and the handheld concept was fully realized by the [[Game Boy]] in 1989. Programmable consoles using swappable cartridges arrived with the Fairchild Channel F in 1976, and the Atari 2600 (1977) popularized them. Consoles are usually sold in generations of five to seven years. Manufacturers often sell hardware at low prices, sometimes at a loss, and profit from licensing fees on each game sold. The market is led by [[Nintendo]], Sony and [[Microsoft]], with their [[PlayStation]] and [[Xbox]] brands, known as the "big three".

Indian film actress. Known for pioneering a change in the portrayal of women in Hindi cinema through female-led films, she won a National Film Award for Best Actress for *The Dirty Picture* (2011) and seven Filmfare Awards. She received the Padma Shri from the [[Government of India]] in 2014. Later films include *Kahaani* (2012), *Shakuntala Devi* (2020) and *Bhool Bhulaiyaa 3* (2024). She is a member of the Indian Central Board of Film Certification and supports women's empowerment.

Capital and largest city of [[Austria]] (pop., 2025: 2,028,289), one of its nine states. It lies on the [[Danube]] at the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods, the northeasternmost foothills of the [[Alps]]. The Romans founded a camp there, called Vindobona, in the 1st century. The Habsburgs made it the seat of the emperors of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] in the 16th century, a role it held until the empire's dissolution in 1806. It was the largest German-speaking city in the 18th and 19th centuries, peaking at two million inhabitants, and was home to composers including [[Ludwig van Beethoven]], [[Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart]] and [[Franz Schubert]]. The historic center was designated a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2001, and Vienna hosts the United Nations and OPEC.

Capital and largest city of [[Laos]] (pop., 2023: 840,000). It stands on the banks of the [[Mekong]] near the border with [[Thailand]], and was the administrative capital during French rule. It is the country's primary administrative, economic and cultural center. The name is the French spelling of the Lao Viangchan. King Setthathirath made the city the capital of [[Lan Xang]] in 1563, to avoid Burmese invasion. Pha That Luang, an icon of Buddhism, stands in the city, as does Haw Phra Kaew, which formerly housed the Emerald Buddha. Vientiane was occupied by Japanese forces during [[World War II]], and French paratroopers reoccupied it in 1946.

Communist-led armed movement and united front in [[South Vietnam]], active 1960–1977. Formed as the National Liberation Front of South Vietnam in 1960, it fought under North Vietnamese direction in the [[Vietnam War]]. Its supporters described it as an indigenous insurgency; the U.S. and South Vietnamese governments portrayed it as a tool of North Vietnam. Its best-known action, the [[Tet Offensive]] of 1968, was an assault on more than 100 South Vietnamese towns and cities. It merged with the Fatherland Front of Vietnam on February 4, 1977, after North and South Vietnam were unified under a communist government.

Conflict in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, c. 1955–1975. North Vietnam, supported by [[China]] and the [[Soviet Union]], fought [[South Vietnam]] and its ally, the [[United States]], while directing the [[Viet Cong]] insurgency in the south. The war was a postcolonial war of national liberation, a theater of the [[Cold War]] and a civil war. U.S. military involvement escalated from 1965 and peaked in 1969. The [[Tet Offensive]] of 1968 was a tactical defeat, but it contributed to growing American opposition to the war. U.S. forces withdrew after the 1973 Paris Peace Accords, and Saigon fell to North Vietnamese forces in 1975. Estimates of Vietnamese soldiers and civilians killed range from 970,000 to 3 million, and 58,220 U.S. service members died. Postwar repression and economic policies helped precipitate the Vietnamese boat people and Indochina refugee crisis, in which about 250,000 perished at sea.

Tonal, isolating Austroasiatic language, the official language of [[Vietnam]]. It is spoken natively by around 86 million people and as a second language by 11 million, and belongs to the Vietic subgroup of the Austroasiatic family. Its syntax is strictly subject–verb–object, and its morphemes are predominantly monosyllabic. Sino-Vietnamese vocabulary, borrowed from Middle Chinese, makes up a significant part of the lexicon. Vietnamese is written in chữ Quốc ngữ, a Latin-based alphabet that relies on 17th-century Portuguese orthography and was officially adopted in the early 20th century during French rule. It was historically written in chữ Nôm, a script built from [[Chinese characters]] and locally created characters.

Late medieval Hindu empire of southern India (1336–1646). It rose after the [[Delhi Sultanate]]'s incursions into the Deccan disrupted the region, and was founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty. Under [[Krishnadevaraya]] (r. 1509–1529) it held primacy across the peninsula, and at its greatest extent it included much of present-day [[Karnataka]], [[Andhra Pradesh]], [[Tamil Nadu]] and [[Goa]]. Its capital, Vijayanagara near modern Hampi, gave the empire its name, and its ruins are a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. Central authority declined after its defeat by allied Deccan Sultanates at the Battle of Talikota in 1565, and the empire survived until 1646. Courts patronized literature in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit, and [[Carnatic music]] developed its classical framework during this era.

Scandinavian seafarers, raiders, traders and settlers, active from the late 8th to the late 11th centuries. They voyaged to the Mediterranean, North Africa, the Middle East and North America, and established Norse settlements in the British Isles, the Faroe Islands, [[Iceland]], [[Greenland]] and [[Normandy]]. Along the Dnieper and Volga trade routes they were known as Varangians, and a group of Rus Vikings attacked [[Constantinople]]. They briefly settled at [[Vinland]], in Newfoundland, and were the first Europeans to reach North America. Their activity profoundly affected early medieval [[England]] and parts of France, and led to the establishment of [[Kievan Rus']]. Most Vikings were farmers, fishermen, craftsmen and traders, and there is no evidence that they wore horned helmets, a costume element that first appeared in the 19th century.

Hungarian lawyer and politician, prime minister of [[Hungary]] 1998–2002 and 2010–2026. He has been president of Fidesz since 2003, having previously led the party from 1993 to 2000. His first government oversaw Hungary's accession to [[NATO]]. The European Commission and Freedom House described changes made after 2010 as weakening judicial independence and media pluralism. Orbán called his model an "illiberal state". He lost the 2026 parliamentary election to Péter Magyar's Tisza Party, and a subsequent constitutional amendment barred him from returning to the prime ministry through a two-term limit.

Italian [[Polymath|polymath]] and economist. Trained in [[Physics]] and [[Mathematics]], he worked as a [[Civil engineering|civil engineer]] before turning seriously to economics in his mid-forties. In 1893 he succeeded Léon Walras at the University of Lausanne, where he remained for the rest of his life. He introduced the concept of Pareto efficiency and helped develop [[Microeconomics]]. He was the first to claim that income follows a Pareto distribution, a power-law [[Probability distribution|probability distribution]]. In 1906 he observed that 20% of the population owned 80% of the property in Italy; this was later generalized into the [[Pareto principle]], or 80–20 rule. He also contributed to [[Sociology|sociology]] and popularized the term elite in social analysis.

Lithuanian Jewish Talmudist, halakhist and [[Kabbalah|kabbalist]], also called Elijah ben Solomon Zalman. Born in Sielec, in the Brest Litovsk Voivodeship of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], he showed extraordinary talent as a child and was consulted on difficult halakhic questions by the age of twenty. Through annotations and emendations of Talmudic and other texts, he became one of the most influential figures in rabbinic study since the [[Middle Ages]]. He joined the Misnagdim, rabbis opposing the influence of [[Hasidic Judaism]]. He advocated secular studies such as mathematics to better understand rabbinic texts, but harshly condemned the study of philosophy and [[Metaphysics]]. The minhag named after him is upheld by many yeshivas and is considered by many the prevailing custom among Ashkenazi Jews in [[Jerusalem]]. None of his manuscripts was published in his lifetime.

Capital and largest city of [[Lithuania]] (pop., 2026: 619,405) and the most populous city in the [[Baltic states]]. Its Old Town is considered one of Europe's largest and best-preserved, and the city was declared a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1994. The Vilnian Baroque style is named after the city, which is the easternmost Baroque city and the largest north of the Alps. The city has been the capital since at least 1323, when Grand Duke [[Gediminas]] first named it as such in a letter. Before World War II it was one of Europe's most important Jewish centers, leading [[Napoleon]] to call it "the Jerusalem of the North" in 1812. It hosted the 2023 [[NATO]] Summit.

American screenwriter, producer and director. He created the AMC crime series *Breaking Bad* (2008–2013) and its prequel *Better Call Saul* (2015–2022). He wrote, directed and produced episodes of *The X-Files*, co-creating its spin-off *The Lone Gunmen*, and co-wrote the superhero film *Hancock* (2008). He has won five Primetime Emmy Awards and six Writers Guild of America Awards. Born in [[Richmond, Virginia]], he studied film at [[New York University]]. In 2025 he created the Apple TV science fiction series *Pluribus*.

American businessman and former professional wrestling promoter. He co-founded the modern [[WWE]] with his wife Linda and bought it from his father in 1982. He came close to monopolizing the [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestling]] industry, creating WrestleMania, which became the world's most successful professional wrestling event. WWE bought World Championship Wrestling in 2001. McMahon resigned from TKO Group Holdings in January 2024 after allegations of sex trafficking and sexual assault. In 2025 he settled SEC charges over undisclosed hush-money payments, without admitting or denying the findings.

American boxer and [[Organized crime|mobster]], boss of the Genovese crime family of [[New York City]] from 1981 to 2005. He fought 25 professional matches before becoming a Mafia enforcer. He was the gunman in the failed 1957 assassination of [[Frank Costello]]. For almost thirty years he feigned insanity, wandering Greenwich Village in a bathrobe and slippers to avoid prosecution. He was convicted of racketeering in 1997, and in 2003 pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice, admitting that the insanity was an act. He died in federal custody in 2005.

American actor, known for villainous roles in [[Horror film|horror films]]. He appeared in more than 100 films, including *House of Wax* (1953) and *The Fly* (1958), and collaborated with Roger Corman on a series of [[Edgar Allan Poe]] adaptations. He played Egghead in the television series *Batman* and voiced Professor Ratigan in *The Great Mouse Detective* (1986). He provided narration for [[Michael Jackson]]'s song "Thriller". He lectured and wrote on art, and the Vincent Price Art Museum at East Los Angeles College is named after him. He has two stars on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

Sour liquid of dilute [[Acetic acid|acetic acid]] and water, used mainly in cooking and as a household cleaner. It is produced by two [[Fermentation|fermentations]]: [[Yeast]] converts sugars to [[Ethanol|ethanol]], and acetic acid bacteria then convert the ethanol into acetic acid. The first documented vinegar making was by the ancient Babylonians around 3000 BC, and in China production was professionalized during the [[Zhou dynasty]]. In the late Middle Ages the French city of Orléans became known for a formalized fermentation and aging process, and malt vinegar developed in England. In 1823 Karl Sebastian Schüzenbach invented the first large-scale industrial process, in the Kingdom of Baden. Vinegar is now used in cooking, as a salad dressing and [[Pickling|pickling]] agent, and in many industrial applications.

Coastal area of North America explored by Norse [[Vikings]]. Named in the Vinland sagas, it lay beyond Greenland and Markland; [[Leif Erikson]] landed there around AD 1000, nearly five centuries before [[Christopher Columbus]]. In 1960 Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad discovered Norse buildings at L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland, proving pre-Columbian Norse exploration of mainland North America. Butternuts found at the site suggest voyages as far as the [[Gulf of St. Lawrence]]. The etymology is disputed; "wine" is usually assumed.

Mountain massif in the Sentinel Range of the Ellsworth Mountains, [[Antarctica]]. It is 21 km (13 mi) long and 13 km (8 mi) wide, and overlooks the Ronne Ice Shelf about 1,200 kilometers (750 mi) from the [[South Pole]]. It contains Mount Vinson, the highest peak in Antarctica at 4,892 meters (16,050 ft). U.S. Navy aircraft discovered the massif in January 1958, and it was named in 1961 after Carl G. Vinson, a [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] congressman who supported Antarctic exploration. Mount Vinson was first climbed in 1966 by an American team led by Nicholas Clinch. Its rocks include quartzose sandstones with [[Devonian]] fossils and Late Cambrian [[Trilobite|trilobites]].

American actress and film producer. She won two Tony Awards for August Wilson plays, *King Hedley II* (2001) and *Fences* (2010). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for reprising her *Fences* role in the 2016 film adaptation. She was the first Black actress to win the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series, for *How to Get Away with Murder*. Her audiobook narration of her memoir *Finding Me* won a Grammy Award, and her accolades include both the Triple Crown of Acting and EGOT.

Bowed string instrument of the violin family, the middle or alto voice of the family. Slightly larger than the [[Violin]] and tuned a perfect fifth below it, the viola has a lower sound; its strings are typically tuned to C3, G3, D4 and A4. The name derives from the Italian *viola da braccio* ("of the arm"). Its music is written mainly in the alto clef. The viola often plays the inner voices in string quartets and symphonic writing, and it occasionally takes a major solo role, as in [[Richard Strauss]]'s symphonic poem *Don Quixote* and [[Hector Berlioz]]'s *Harold en Italie*. Concertos by [[Béla Bartók]], Paul Hindemith, Georg Philipp Telemann and William Walton are considered major works of the repertoire.

Genus of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family Violaceae, commonly known as violets. It is the largest genus in its family, with over 680 species, mostly in the temperate Northern Hemisphere, though some occur in [[Hawaii]], Australasia and the [[Andes]]. Some species are perennial, some annual, and a few are small shrubs. Many are grown in gardens for their ornamental flowers; in horticulture, "pansy" normally refers to multicolored, large-flowered cultivars raised annually or biennially from seed. The flowers are strongly zygomorphic, with five petals, and some species have an elusive scent, largely from [[Ketone|ionone]], a ketone that temporarily desensitizes the nose's receptors. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described the genus in 1753 with 19 species.

Color of light at the short-wavelength end of the [[Visible spectrum|visible spectrum]], with wavelengths of about 380–435 nm. It was one of the seven colors that [[Isaac Newton]] labeled in 1704. The name derives from the [[Viola (plant)|Viola]] genus of flowers, and the first recorded use as a color name in English was in 1370. In the [[RGB color model|RGB]] model, violet is produced by mixing red and blue light, with more blue than red. [[Tyrian purple]] dye was extremely expensive in antiquity, which gave violet a long association with royalty. In Chinese painting, violet represents "unity transcending the duality of yin and yang."

Wooden chordophone, the smallest and highest-pitched instrument in regular use in the violin family. Most violins have four strings, usually tuned in perfect fifths to G3, D4, A4 and E5, and are played mainly with a bow. First created in 16th-century Italy, the violin is central to Western classical music, in [[Orchestra|orchestras]] and as a solo instrument, and is also important in [[Folk music|folk]], [[Country music|country]] and [[Jazz|jazz]] music. Violins by [[Antonio Stradivari]], and by the Guarneri, Guadagnini and Amati families, made in Brescia and Cremona, are especially prized, though the belief that their sound cannot be equaled is disputed. Stradivari alone made more than 1,100 instruments, of which about 650 survive. Often called a fiddle, the instrument is also incorporated into many non-Western traditions, including Indian and Iranian music.
